notes.meaning: Jesus called his twelve disciples together and gave them power over evil spirits and every kind of sickness. The number twelve mirrored the twelve tribes of Israel, showing that Jesus was appointing leaders for God's renewed people. He shared his own authority with them so they could heal people and show that God's kingdom had arrived.

Matthew lists the names of the twelve apostles, beginning with Simon Peter and his brother Andrew, and then James and John. The word apostle means a messenger sent out with the authority of the sender. Peter is listed first because he served as the natural leader and chief speaker for the group.

differ.view: Peter was first in order and honor among the disciples, but he held no governing authority over the other apostles.
Peter is listed first simply because he was called early or acted as group spokesman, not because he held higher rank.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Peter is named first because Christ gave him supreme authority and leadership as head of the earthly church.

notes.meaning: The list continues with Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, Matthew the tax collector, James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus. Bartholomew is likely another name for Nathanael, who was brought to Jesus by Philip. Matthew openly mentions his despised former job as a tax collector to highlight God's unearned grace in choosing him.

The final two apostles named in the list are Simon the Zealot and Judas Iscariot. Simon had belonged to a patriotic Jewish group that fought passionately for national independence and the law of Moses. Judas is identified from the beginning as the one who would later betray Jesus.

Jesus sent the twelve out with orders not to visit Gentile territory or enter Samaritan cities. The Samaritans had mixed ancestry and worshiped apart from Jerusalem, creating centuries of bitter hostility with the Jews. Jesus set this temporary limit so his followers would focus their first efforts entirely on the Jewish nation.

Jesus directed the apostles to go instead to the lost sheep of Israel. He saw the Jewish people as helpless sheep who had strayed because their spiritual leaders had neglected them. Because they were God's ancient chosen people, the good news was offered to them first.

Wherever the disciples traveled, their main assignment was to announce that the kingdom of heaven was near. They carried the exact same urgent message that John the Baptist and Jesus had been proclaiming throughout Galilee. They acted as royal heralds, calling people to turn back to God and prepare for his rule.

Jesus instructed them to heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, and cast out demons. These miracles proved to the crowds that the apostles spoke with divine authority. Because God gave them this power freely, they were forbidden from charging money for their ministry.

The disciples were told not to carry any gold, silver, or copper coins in their money belts. They were to set out immediately rather than waiting to save up funds for the journey. This command taught them to step out in faith and depend on God for their daily needs.

Jesus also told them not to take a food bag, extra clothes, spare sandals, or a spare walking stick. God's workers have a right to receive their food and shelter from the people they serve. Traveling light kept them free from distractions and allowed them to move quickly.

When arriving in any town, the disciples were to seek out a godly host who was ready to welcome their message. Once welcomed, they were to stay in that same house until they left for the next town. Moving from home to home in search of better comforts would make them look greedy and hurt their work.

As the messengers entered a home, they were to offer the family a blessing of peace. In Jewish life, this greeting was more than a polite hello; it asked God to shower his favor and salvation on the household. Showing warmth and respect helped open hearts to the gospel message.

If the family welcomed the disciples and their message, God's peace would rest upon that home. If the household rejected them, that blessing would return to the apostles rather than staying with the family. God offers his grace freely, but he will not force his peace on those who turn it away.

If a home or town refused to welcome the apostles or hear their words, they were to shake the dust off their feet as they departed. Jewish travelers performed this act when leaving foreign lands to avoid bringing pagan uncleanness back home. Doing this to a Jewish town visibly showed that rejecting Christ cut people off from God's blessings.

Jesus warned that towns refusing the gospel would face a harsher judgment than Sodom and Gomorrah. God destroyed those ancient cities for their terrible wickedness, but they never received the light of Christ's messengers. People who turn away from greater truth and mercy bear a far heavier guilt.

Jesus warned his disciples that he was sending them out like defenseless sheep into a pack of wolves. To survive, they had to be as shrewd as snakes in avoiding traps, yet as innocent as doves by never causing harm. Wisdom and gentleness had to go together so they would neither create trouble nor fall into it.

Jesus cautioned the disciples to watch out for hostile opponents who would seek to stop them. Local leaders would arrest them, drag them before town courts, and have them whipped inside the synagogues. Faithful believers had to understand that serious opposition would often come from religious authorities.

The apostles would eventually be put on trial before Roman governors and kings for following Jesus. These hearings were not accidents, but divine opportunities to witness to high officials and foreign nations. God often uses seasons of trial to bring his message before people who would never otherwise hear it.

When placed on trial, the disciples were told not to worry about what to say or how to say it. God promised to give them the exact words they needed in that very hour. This promise brought deep comfort to humble fishermen who had to face powerful rulers.

In those critical moments, the disciples would not have to speak by their own wisdom. The Holy Spirit of their Heavenly Father would speak directly through them. God equips his people and personally stands by them whenever they are called to defend the truth.

Jesus warned that following him would divide families, leading brothers, parents, and children to hand one another over to be put to death. Deep hatred toward the gospel would break even the closest ties of natural affection. Jesus prepared his disciples ahead of time so they would not be shattered when faith provoked painful family opposition.
